name: Saint Anselm
history: An Italian who became abbot of Bec in Normandy and then Archbishop of Canterbury, Anselm was the greatest theologian of his age. He described his work as faith seeking understanding, and wrote the Proslogion and Why God Became Man. Twice exiled for defending the freedom of the Church, he was named a Doctor of the Church in 1720.
life: Born at Aosta, Anselm left home after a quarrel with his father and crossed the Alps to the abbey of Bec, drawn by the fame of its prior, Lanfranc. He became a monk there in 1060, then prior and abbot, and was loved as a gentle and patient teacher. At Bec he wrote the Monologion and the Proslogion, in which he speaks of God as that than which nothing greater can be thought. In 1093, during a visit to England, he was made Archbishop of Canterbury against his will, the crozier pressed into his closed hand. He clashed with William Rufus and then Henry I over the rights of the Church, and spent years in exile. At the Council of Bari in 1098 he defended the Western teaching on the Holy Spirit. In exile he finished Cur Deus Homo, on why God became man. He died at Canterbury on 21 April 1109.
prayerTo: Saint Anselm, you sought to understand what you believed, and to love what you understood. Pray for theologians, for students and for the Church in England. Teach me to seek God with my mind and my heart, and to find, in seeking Him, that He has already found me. Amen.
penance: Give a quarter of an hour today to thinking about God in silence: sit with one line of the Creed and ask Him to show you more.
meditation: I do not seek to understand in order to believe, he wrote, but I believe in order to understand. What do you believe that you would like to understand better?
prayer: O God, who didst give blessed Anselm to be thy people’s minister in eternal salvation; grant, we pray, that we who have him for teacher of life here on earth, may also deserve now that he is in heaven, to have him for an advocate. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
prayerSource: Collect of the day, Roman Missal of 1962
